x: The ground station The ground station is one program that drives the three vehicles over MAVLink, reports to the judges over the RoboCommand protocol, and keeps enough state to resume a task after an interruption.

Architecture The vehicles communicate over MAVLink. The ground station communicates with RoboCommand over MQTT with protocol buffer payloads. Between the two is one orchestrator that holds all mission state. The terminal console, the three dimensional course view and the protocol client all read from it. Ground station architecture. Only the RoboCommand client connects to the course network, as handbook 3.4 requires. The vehicles do not connect to the judges' broker. A simulated vehicle, a firmware build running software in the loop and a real vehicle all implement the same adapter interface, so the mission code does not depend on which one it is driving.

State machines Mission state is held in three state machines. What each machine owns. Machine One per States Vehicle vehicle OFFLINE, BOOTING, READY, AUTONOMOUS, TASK_EXECUTING, RETURNING, EMERGENCY_STOP Task task attempt INACTIVE, QUEUED, ASSIGNED, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETE, FAILED, ABORTED Mission run IDLE, PRE_RUN_CHECK, RUNNING, EMERGENCY, COMPLETE Each task also carries an ordered list of steps. The console shows these as a previous, current and next triple. A step is the smallest unit the mission can be resumed at.

Interrupt and resume This design is for Task 4. RoboCommand can interrupt a run at any time with an assistance request, a keep-out zone or a moving vessel. The vehicle in the affected domain has to acknowledge the message, stop its current task, respond to the incident, and then continue. When an incident arrives the orchestrator writes a checkpoint: the task, the step it reached, the progress through the step list and the score events already earned. The vehicle then runs the incident as its own task. When the incident clears, the checkpoint is restored and the vehicle continues from the step it stopped on, not from the start of the task. Your browser cannot play this video. Download it instead . A keep-out zone arrives during the transit. The console acknowledges it, the boat routes around the area, and the safe passage attempt resumes afterwards.

Health and escalation A heartbeat monitor checks every vehicle. Missed heartbeats and low battery raise alerts. Sustained heartbeat loss escalates to an emergency stop automatically, without waiting for the operator. Battery thresholds are set per vehicle, because 20 percent on a quadrotor is more urgent than 20 percent on a boat. Before a run the console can run a pre-run check: every vehicle reachable and in a ready state, every battery above its minimum, and all three domains present. The check changes nothing and can also be run during a mission.

Operator console The console is a terminal application. It runs over a shell connection from a laptop in the team's tent on the promontory, it does not need a browser, and it redraws correctly over a slow link. The layout is fixed so the operator always finds the same value in the same place. +- Header (clock) ------------------------------------------------------------+ | ROBOTX 2026 | IDLE -> [RUNNING] -> COMPLETE | Tier: ADVANCED | RC: * 04:12 | +--- USV ----------------+--- UUV ---------------+--- UAV ---------------------+ | USV > SAFE_PASSAGE | UUV | UAV > SAFE_PASSAGE | | READY -> [TASK_EXEC] | AUTONOMOUS | AUTONOMOUS -> [TASK_EXEC] | | Step: ROUTE_RELAY | Step: - | Step: [ROUTE_RELAY] | | Pos: 1.2834,103.8607 | Depth: 1.4 m | Alt: 42 m | | Batt: [#######...] 73% | Batt: [########..] 81%| Batt: [#########.] 92% | +- Task Prev -> [Current] -> Next Tier Vehicles ----------------+ | SAFE_PASSAGE ASSIGNED -> [IN_PROGRESS] ADV usv,uav | | Step: ROUTE_RELAY -> [TRANSIT_PASSAGE] -> EXIT_REPORT ########.. 72% | | INFRASTRUCTURE_SURVEY - -> [QUEUED] ADV uuv,uav | +- Incident panel (only while a Task 4 incident is live) ---------------------+ +- Health and alerts ------------------+- RoboCommand log --------------------+ | [OK ] USV heartbeat 8 ms | 14:22:01 -> DockingReport bay=2 | | [WARN] UAV battery low: 28.1% | 14:22:00 <- RxCommand run_start | +--------------------------------------+--------------------------------------+ F1 ESTOP F2 Abort F3 Pre-Check F4 Arm F5 T4-Core F6 T4-Adv F7 T4-Dis The same mission can also be opened in a browser at the same time, in the three dimensional view on the simulation page. The terminal is the control interface and the browser view is for watching.

RoboCommand link Handbook 3.4 defines how teams report to the judges: MQTT over TCP on port 1883, protocol buffer payloads from RoboNation's schema release, four topics, and a run start handshake that has to complete before the run begins. Our client implements the protocol, and we have tested it against RoboNation's test server. The four topics, from handbook 3.4.7. Purpose Topic Direction Course configuration robocommand/robotx/course To us, retained Vehicle report robocommand/robotx/SUTD/<vehicle>/report From us Team request robocommand/robotx/SUTD/request From us Team command robocommand/robotx/SUTD/command To us Reports go out at 2 Hz per vehicle carrying state, position, speed, heading, roll, pitch, altitude or depth, current task and vehicle type, with flight phase added for the aircraft. Sequence numbers are per vehicle for reports and per team for requests, and a response quotes the sequence number of the message it answers. The run start sequence and the log it produced are described step by step on the proof of readiness page.

Design decisions Three state machines instead of one A vehicle can be autonomous while its task is suspended and the mission is in an emergency. A single machine would need a state for every combination. Checkpoints outside the task machine An interruption resets the task machine, so the checkpoint has to be stored outside it. Resume then restores the saved data instead of replaying the task. Depth hold counts as autonomous This applies only to the underwater vehicle, which has no position estimate to hold. The other two vehicles have to be in a guided mode to count. Only the consumed streams are requested ArduPilot's default stream set would saturate a HaLow link. The adapter requests position at 4 Hz and status at 1 Hz, and requests them again if telemetry stops. The ground station has 154 automated tests covering the state machines, the orchestrator lifecycle, suspend and resume, the protocol end to end, the embedded broker, the course layout and the readiness rehearsal. See the test record .

Team introduction video The team has twenty six students working on simulation, computer vision, planning, control, electronics, communications and the aircraft, with Prof. Malika Meghjani as advisor. This is the team introduction video for the 2026 challenge. Team members and groups

The mission The 2026 scenario is a storm response at a coastal port. The four RobotX tasks are run as one operation, and each task needs more than one vehicle. 1. Safe passage Ten buoys carry light beacons. At the Advanced tier the route can only be seen from above. The quadrotor reads the field, reports it to RoboCommand and sends the entry, exit and marker positions to the boat before the boat transits. 2. Infrastructure survey and repair The ROV homes on the active pinger, follows the pipeline, classifies each segment as intact or damaged, and holds its magnetic probe on the damaged node. The repaired node then shows which resource it needs, and the quadrotor delivers it. 3. Coordinated logistics The boat finds the green docking bay, docks, sprays the lit window until it turns green, then sends the delivery colour to the quadrotor. 4. Dynamic incident response RoboCommand interrupts the run with an assistance request, a keep-out zone or a moving vessel. The affected vehicle acknowledges the message, responds, then resumes its task at the step where it stopped.

The vehicles Three vehicles, each running ArduPilot, all reached through the same MAVLink interface. The ground station uses the same code for a simulated vehicle, a firmware build and the real hardware. Surface BlueBoat A 1.2 m catamaran on ArduPilot Rover, with shrouded thrusters, a wireless kill switch and a 360 degree status light. It transits the safe passage, docks, sprays the window, and carries the surface link for the ROV. Autopilot ArduPilot Rover Link to shore WiFi HaLow, MAVLink Tasks 1, 3, 4 BlueBoat in detail Subsurface BlueROV2 A six thruster ROV on ArduPilot Sub. It has no DVL, so it has no absolute position underwater and runs in depth hold mode instead of guided mode. The underwater software is designed around this. Autopilot ArduPilot Sub, BlueOS companion Camera RTSP, 1280x720 at 15 fps Tasks 2, 4 BlueROV2 in detail Air 22 inch quadrotor Built in the lab on ArduPilot Copter, 6.8 kg in the delivery configuration, with foam flotation so it can be recovered after a ditching. It reads the buoy field from above, sends the route to the boat, and carries resource tins to the platforms. The ground station The ground station runs the mission. It commands the vehicles over MAVLink, communicates with the judges over the RoboCommand protocol, and checkpoints every task so that an interruption costs a few seconds instead of the run. Task 4, Advanced. RoboCommand issues a keep-out zone during the run. The operator console acknowledges it, the boat routes around the area, and the suspended task resumes at the step it stopped on. Mission state machines Three state machines run in parallel: one per vehicle, one per task, one for the mission. The task machine handles suspend and resume, so Task 4 uses the same mechanism as any other interruption. Protocol testing The operator console ran the handbook's run start sequence against RoboNation's rc-test server. The log we submitted was written by their decoder. Course model Marina Bay, the buoy field, the pipeline and the docking bays are modelled to the handbook's build specifications. We use the model to rehearse a run before the hardware is on the water. Proof of readiness A vehicle may only operate at RobotX 2026 after its readiness submission has passed. Handbook section 3.1 asks for a recorded autonomous run per domain, drawings and photographs of the safety systems, and a log of a run start sequence. Software in the loop Software in the loop runs the same firmware the vehicles run, compiled for the laptop: ArduRover with a motorboat model for the BlueBoat, ArduSub with a vectored model for the ROV, and Copter with a quad model for the aircraft. The arming checks, filter convergence, guided navigation and failsafes are the firmware's own. Between the firmware and the ground station is an emulator for the WiFi HaLow link. It adds fixed latency and jitter, random loss, a bandwidth cap and periodic outages. Link profiles. Profile Behaviour perfect No impairment. Used for tests that are not about the link. halow_near Short range, low latency, occasional loss. halow_typical The link expected on the course. halow_fringe 60 ms of latency with 40 ms of jitter, 8 percent loss, 300 kbps, and a two second fade every 25 seconds. Under the fringe profile the health monitor escalates to an emergency stop on heartbeat loss, which is the intended behaviour. Testing under this profile is also why the adapter now requests only the telemetry it uses instead of ArduPilot's default stream set.

Course model The course objects are built from the handbook's build specifications, in metres: ten buoys with side and top light beacons, the pair of survey buoys with their colour indicators and pingers, a five section pipeline on stands with five magnetic light nodes, three docking bays with their windows and indicators, two 2 m delivery platforms with 65 cm circles in the specified colours, and the launch pad. Marina Bay Sands, the ArtScience Museum, the Singapore Flyer and the Helix Bridge are included as landmarks, since they are what the operator sees from the course. End to end validation One command launches the fleet, runs a full scripted mission against it and prints a pass or fail table of 25 checks. The sequence runs from a cold start to a stop: fleet ready with position, the pre-run gate, the course configuration and run declaration, arming against real prearm checks, run start, takeoff, task dispatch, buoy circling and the passage transit under guided navigation, an assistance request arriving mid transit, the checkpoint, the incident response with its acknowledgement on the wire, resume from the checkpoint, the safe passage report, task and mission completion, return to launch, and an emergency stop that disarms everything. The exit code is used in continuous integration, so a change that breaks the mission fails the build. The browser scene is checked the same way. A headless test builds the scene without a display, runs the mission, and fails if a task does not complete, if the expected RoboCommand messages do not appear in order, if a chase camera loses its vehicle, or if the underwater chase camera comes above the surface.

What is simulated Real components The autopilot firmware, its arming and failsafe logic, the MQTT broker, the protocol buffer schema from the competition release, the message rates, and the ground station. The same program drives the simulated fleet and the hardware. Simplified or missing Vehicle dynamics are limited to the firmware's own models. Waves, current and cameras are not modelled. Perception cannot be tested in this setup, so the detector work is tested on recorded footage.

Planned work Two additions are planned. Tasks 2 and 3 will get their own validation scenarios, so the pipeline follow and the dock approach are tested the same way as the safe passage. After that, a Gazebo world with the course props would add simulated cameras and disturbances, which perception in the loop testing needs. Photorealistic underwater rendering in Isaac Sim was evaluated and not adopted. The lab's current graphics card is not supported by the versions with the underwater features, and the mission logic does not need it.

The team MARVL is the Multi-Agent Robotics Vision and Learning Lab at the Singapore University of Technology and Design. RobotX 2026 is a lab-wide project covering the software, three vehicle builds and the safety documentation.

Who we are MARVL works on mobile robotics, multi-robot coordination, planning and scheduling, computer vision and machine learning, with field robotics on marine, ground and aerial platforms. The lab has operated surface and underwater vehicles in Singapore waters for several years. RobotX 2026 is the first time the lab has run all three domains together as one system. The competition entry is a student team under the RoboNation eligibility rules: at least three quarters of the members are full-time students, and students do the engineering. Staff and alumni advise. Buoyancy test. The aircraft has to float and be recoverable after a ditching. We tested this in the pool and recovered it by hand.

How the team is organised Two leads run the project under the faculty advisor. The work is split into nine groups, and most members are in more than one, because much of the work crosses group boundaries: a detector has to feed the planner, and a controller has to be checked in simulation first. All of the groups deliver into the ground station, which is the one piece of software that talks to all three vehicles and to RoboCommand. Simulation The ArduPilot software in the loop fleet, the HaLow link emulator, the Marina Bay course model and the scripted validation run. Computer vision Buoy, beacon, pipeline and docking bay detection, camera work on the ROV and the aircraft, and the datasets behind them. Planning Mission orchestration, the task state machines, checkpointing and the Task 4 interruption handling. Control Autopilot configuration and tuning on all three vehicles, guided and depth hold modes, and the failsafes. Electronics Power, the kill switch chain, the status lights, payload wiring and the companion computers. Communication The WiFi HaLow link, the RoboCommand client, RF declarations and the network on the course. Design documentation The technical design report, this website and the proof of readiness packages. UAV The airframe build, flight testing, the delivery mechanism, pilot licensing and the airworthiness case with CAAS. UUV BlueROV2 integration, depth control, the magnetic probe and the pipeline survey.

Test record We test at three levels: an automated suite, simulated missions against the real firmware, and sessions with the hardware in the water and in the air. This page lists what has been run, its objective and its result.

Test levels Hardware time is limited. A pool booking takes a morning, a boat session takes a day, and the aircraft needs a licensed pilot present. We find as many problems as possible in software and simulation first, and use field sessions for the tests that need water or air. Automated suite, every commit The suite runs in about a minute and covers the mission logic, the protocol and the course model. Simulated mission, before a hardware session The mission runs end to end against the real firmware over an emulated radio, with a pass or fail per stage. Hardware sessions Autonomy, safety systems and failsafes are tested on the water and in the air. Each session is recorded from start to finish, and the footage is used as readiness evidence.

Software suite The suite has 154 tests. The last full run took 53 seconds and passed 153. The remaining test is the software in the loop round trip, which is opt in because it builds and boots firmware. Automated tests by area, as of 21 September 2026. What testing changed These test results led to design changes. Underwater vehicle position ArduSub does not allow guided modes without a position estimate, and the vehicle has no position estimate underwater. Depth hold is now used as the autonomous mode for that vehicle, and the survey is flown on heading and time with visual reacquisition. Telemetry load on the radio The default telemetry set overloaded the emulated link under the fringe profile. The adapter now requests position at 4 Hz and status at 1 Hz, and requests again if telemetry stops. This is a few packets per second per vehicle. Arming delay The filter needs 20 to 40 seconds after boot before prearm passes, and the position prearm check is the usual failure on the boat. Arming now retries for 90 seconds instead of failing the run. Guided waypoint timeout One check in the validation run fails: a guided waypoint on the boat does not report arrival inside its window, usually after the vehicle has been through an interruption. The mission still completes, so the cause is the acceptance window and retry logic, not navigation. This is the next item being worked on. Reuse of the 2024 detector The trained buoy model still works for the colour classes at 0.945 mAP@0.5. The shape classes do not transfer, because the 2026 buoys carry light beacons instead of shapes.

Planned tests before November Pipeline survey in water with the magnetic probe, including a repair hold on a mock light node. Docking approach and the water jet against a built docking bay. Delivery mechanism flights: pick a tin, fly a route, release on a circle. One session with all three vehicles autonomous at the same time, reporting through the ground station to a local broker. Validation scenarios for Tasks 2 and 3 alongside the existing Task 1 run. Fix the guided waypoint timeout so the validation run passes 25 of 25.

22 inch quadrotor The aerial vehicle, a quadrotor built in the lab on ArduPilot Copter. It maps the buoy field from above, relays the route to the boat, and carries resource tins to the delivery platforms. It is fitted with flotation because the course is over water.

Airframe The airframe is a custom 22 inch quadrotor with carbon arms and plate, 22.4 by 8 inch two blade propellers, and foam flotation strapped along the arms and the body. The flotation keeps the aircraft upright and recoverable after a ditching. Two configurations are declared: the base aircraft, and the base aircraft with the tin grabbing assembly fitted. Power and endurance Four 6S1P lithium ion packs in parallel, 4,500 mAh each, 18,000 mAh at 22.2 V in total. Flight testing at the delivery configuration mass gives about 18 minutes, so missions are planned to land by 15 with roughly three minutes in reserve. Control and telemetry The manual link is a RadioMaster transmitter with a built in ExpressLRS module, paired to a receiver on the aircraft. It is independent of the ground station, so the pilot can take off, fly and land with the laptop switched off. The ground station runs Mission Planner for monitoring, mission upload and autonomous mission management. The operator console reports the aircraft to RoboCommand at 2 Hz, the same as the other two vehicles. Manual link ExpressLRS 2.4 GHz, frequency hopping Transmit power 50 mW setting, about 0.08 W EIRP Telemetry 2.4 GHz to Mission Planner Flight modes Stabilise, AltHold, Loiter, Auto, Land, RTL Declared ceiling 50 m above mean sea level Geofence Polygon with a 4 m internal buffer Aircraft telemetry is also relayed to meet Singapore's network remote identification requirements, so every heartbeat has to carry the complete field set. This is one reason the RoboCommand client fills in flight phase, altitude and heading on every report, not only when they change. The dedicated transmitter, assigned to this aircraft and the nominated pilot.

A scored attempt does not resume after a manual takeover The emergency stop on the transmitter cuts the motors immediately, on the ground and in the air. Delivery payload Tasks 2 and 3 both end with a tin placed on a coloured circle. The delivery assembly is a removable tin grabbing mechanism of about 0.20 kg on an underside mount, powered from the main battery. The mount is drilled and the aircraft flies with it fitted. The grabber itself is still being finished. The delivery tins are aluminium cans of 40 to 50 g coated in red, green or blue. The platforms are 2 m squares with 60 to 70 cm circles in the handbook's specified colours. The simulator draws these, and the perception work is trained on them.

BlueBoat The surface vessel. It transits the safe passage, docks, sprays the window in Task 3, and carries the surface link for the underwater vehicle.

The platform The boat is a Blue Robotics BlueBoat, a 1.2 m catamaran with two thrusters, an ArduPilot Rover autopilot, and a companion computer that carries the WiFi HaLow link back to shore. The ground station drives it over MAVLink. The same interface is used in simulation, in software in the loop and on the water. Autonomy The ground station holds the boat in GUIDED and sends position targets. The safe passage transit and the dock approach are both sequences of these targets. Arming goes through ArduPilot's prearm checks with a retry, because a GPS prearm failure is the most common problem on this hull, and the retry usually clears it in about thirty seconds. Under rule 5.1, leaving autonomy ends scoring for the attempt. The console therefore treats a manual takeover as an abort: the run is marked not scoring and the operator sees this in the header. Task 3 adds a dock approach that places the hull inside a bay, and a water jet aimed at a 25 cm window. Both run from the same task state machine as the other tasks, with one step per action, so a suspension during the dock approach resumes at the step it stopped on.

Perception The buoy detector is a YOLOv5s model trained on the MHSeals set, at 0.945 mAP@0.5 and 0.693 mAP@0.5:0.95 over 27 classes. The colour classes apply directly to the 2026 light beacons. The shape classes do not, because the 2026 buoys carry lights instead of shapes. Camera to lidar fusion from the lab's earlier work has about 8 cm of range error and a systematic 8 to 9 cm lateral and vertical bias. The passage transit planning uses this figure as its position uncertainty.

BlueROV2 The underwater vehicle. It surveys the pipeline in Task 2 and repairs the damaged node with a magnetic probe. It has no position source underwater, which shaped how it is controlled.

The platform The vehicle is a BlueROV2 in the heavy configuration, with six thrusters, an ArduPilot Sub autopilot, and a Raspberry Pi running BlueOS that carries video and MAVLink up the tether. The autonomy stack connects on one UDP endpoint and a pilot keeps QGroundControl on another, so the pilot can take over at any time without stopping the autonomy stack. Frame BlueROV2, 0.46 m, six thrusters Autopilot ArduPilot Sub Companion Raspberry Pi, BlueOS at 192.168.2.2 Autonomy endpoint udpin 14551 Pilot endpoint udpin 14550, QGroundControl Camera RTSP H264, 1280x720 at 15 fps

No position underwater ArduSub rejects GUIDED and POSHOLD with "requires position" whenever the filter has no position estimate. In software in the loop this clears about a minute after boot, once the filter starts using GPS. On the real vehicle underwater it never clears, because a BlueROV2 without a Doppler velocity log or an acoustic positioning system has no absolute position source. Adding either sensor was outside the budget, so the ground station treats depth hold as an autonomous mode for this vehicle only. The adapter requests GUIDED first, falls back to depth hold when arming, and drives the vehicle with body frame velocity commands. The autopilot closes the depth loop, which is the one axis it can hold without a position estimate. Consequences The survey is flown on heading and time instead of on waypoints, so the pipeline has to be found again by camera after each turn. In return the vehicle can run autonomously with the hardware it has now, and does not depend on a sensor that may not arrive before the event.

Control interface The adapter sends two kinds of command to the vehicle. The two command paths and when each is used. Command What it does Used for VELOCITY Body frame velocity with yaw rate, in depth hold The normal autonomy path: transit, survey, station keeping RC_OVERRIDE Writes the same channels a pilot's transmitter writes, 1500 neutral, 1100 to 1900 full scale Fine positioning on the pipeline, and handing the vehicle back to a pilot mid-run Channels not named in an override keep the pilot's stick values instead of being zeroed. This lets the pilot take over on the controller without the autonomy commands working against them.

Pipeline survey and repair Task 2 starts at the buoy with the green indicator, which has the active pinger below it. The vehicle descends, finds the pipeline, and reports each of the five segments as intact or damaged, working from that end. The damaged segment has a red light ring with a magnetic switch at its centre. Holding the probe on the switch turns the light green. At Advanced the repaired node then flashes a colour for thirty seconds to name the resource it needs. The vehicle sends that request to the aircraft and reports completion to RoboCommand. At Disruptive the node flashes two colours, the first naming the tin and the second naming the delivery circle, and the request carries both. Survey rehearsal in the simulator. The chase camera stays below the surface while the vehicle is submerged, since a camera above the water would not see it.

Safety systems Onboard kill switch. The vehicle is positively buoyant when killed, so it surfaces. Status light readable at about 80 m while surfaced, showing kill, manual and autonomous. Marked tow and lift points with a harness. A dedicated mounting location for the RJE ULB-350 locator beacon the event issues before any underwater vehicle enters the water, mounted vertically with the end cap down. Tether to the boat kept positively buoyant, under 6 m, and strong enough to recover the vehicle by pulling on it. During a scoring run nothing attached to the vehicle may float on the surface, and the vehicle must not breach. For this reason depth hold is armed before the run starts, not after the first transit.
